value: Food pictures exhibited a significantly stronger activation of the left DLPFC in obese versus normal-weight subjects. This finding was specific for food stimuli, as no DLPFC activation was seen for pleasant pictures.

The increased DLPFC activation in obese children points to an avoidance process associated with the presented food stimuli and suggests that stronger top-down control is necessary to suppress food-related reward responses.

definition.value: Normal weight > overweight during viewing of food stimuli

value: Lean versus obese children showed significantly stronger activations in the ACC, thalamus, caudate, hippocampus/parahippocampal gyrus, and visual cortex during viewing of food pictures.

These results point to increased vigilance in normal-weight children to the presented stimuli. The caudate and hippocampus were more strongly activated during food cues in normal-weight, but not obese, children.

definition.value: Greater activation in the right DLPFC in obese versus normal-weight subjects during food pictures

value: We also found a tendency for greater activation in the right DLPFC in obese versus normal-weight subjects.

The tendency for greater right DLPFC activation was consistent with the significantly stronger left DLPFC activation in obese children during food-cue viewing, although it did not reach the study's significance threshold.

definition.value: Afternoon minus morning sessions during the pleasant condition

value: The left VLPFC activation for afternoon minus morning sessions was not specific for food stimuli, but was also found during the pleasant condition. The authors suggested that this might be associated with a more vivid emotional perception.

label.value: heart rate deceleration evoked by food pictures

spans.text: Heart rate deceleration evoked by food pictures was significantly correlated with the neural activation of a cluster in the VLPFC for the combined group of obese and normal-weight subjects (MNI coordinates: 39, 39, –3; T =3.01; see Figure 2 ).

value: Heart rate deceleration evoked by food pictures was significantly correlated with neural activation of a cluster in the VLPFC for the combined group of obese and normal-weight subjects.

The positive correlation between increased heart rate deceleration and increasing VLPFC activity indicates that the more intense the orienting response to food cues, the greater the activation of the VLPFC.
